title: Pizza with meat (not pepperoni), school lunch, thin crust

content.title: About
content.content: A pizza topped with meat but without pepperoni is a common offering in school cafeterias as a quick and filling lunch. The thin crust (3416) provides a crisp base, while meat pieces such as chicken, beef, or ham add protein. The pizza typically includes tomato sauce, mozzarella cheese, and a modest amount of vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thin crust requires a higher baking temperature, resulting in a crunchy edge.
In school menus pizza is often considered a "fast" dish, but it can be enriched with vegetables for a more balanced meal.
Meat used in school pizzas is usually pre‑cooked (boiled or baked) to ensure food safety.
Tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, which becomes more bioavailable after heating.
Pizza is traditionally cut into triangular slices, making it easy to serve in a cafeteria.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The meat topping provides high‑quality protein essential for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Mozzarella cheese supplies calcium important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Lycopene in sauce
items.content: Cooked tomatoes increase the availability of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The crust delivers quick‑acting carbohydrates for immediate energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and, when used, whole‑grain crust provide B1, B2, B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese and prepared sauce can contain a lot of salt, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Traditional cheese and meat may raise saturated fat intake, relevant for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Dairy and gluten in the crust can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Pizza can be high in calories, so portion control is advisable, especially for children.

items.title: Meat quality control
items.content: Improper storage or insufficient cooking of meat can lead to foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, sliced into triangles. It can be complemented with fresh vegetables (tomatoes, cucumbers) or herbs to boost nutrition. For a healthier option, choose a whole‑grain thin crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in an oven or microwave to restore crispness. Discard if the pizza develops a sour smell or visible mold.
